steps.label: KP01 Neurons and thresholds
KP01 Neurons and thresholds · 1
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate. Chapter 2 KP01. Native teaching-diagram review draft. Several signals arrive. Add their contributions, then test whether the threshold is reached. We will turn this mechanism into a rule we can compute by hand.

steps.label: KP01 Neurons and thresholds · 2
steps.speakerNotes: Add the signals; output one when the threshold is reached.

steps.label: Four parts relay a signal · 1
steps.speakerNotes: Dendrites receive signals. The soma represents integration in this simplified diagram. The axon transmits a pulse, and synapses relay it onward. The artificial model abstracts integration and thresholding.

steps.label: Four parts relay a signal · 2
steps.speakerNotes: Receive, integrate, transmit, relay.

steps.label: Firing is a switch, not a volume knob · 1
steps.speakerNotes: Fix the threshold at two. A sum of one falls short; two reaches it exactly; three exceeds it. The last two both output one. This is a simplified computational mechanism, not a physiological amplitude model.

steps.label: Firing is a switch, not a volume knob · 2
steps.speakerNotes: At or above the threshold, the answer stays one.

steps.label: Weight each input, then add its contribution · 1
steps.speakerNotes: Multiply each input by its weight, then add the products. The symbol d is the number of inputs. The weighted sum z does not yet include the threshold adjustment.

steps.label: Weight each input, then add its contribution · 2
steps.speakerNotes: A weight sets how much an input contributes.

steps.label: Subtract the threshold to compare with zero · 1
steps.speakerNotes: Start by comparing the sum with the threshold. Subtract the threshold from both sides to compare with zero instead. Calling the negative threshold the bias gives sum plus bias. Both marked positions shift equally, so their distance is unchanged.

steps.label: Subtract the threshold to compare with zero · 2
steps.speakerNotes: The bias is the negative threshold.

steps.label: The step function turns a sum into zero or one · 1
steps.speakerNotes: The negative half-axis outputs zero; the nonnegative half-axis outputs one. At zero, the lower point is open and the upper point is filled. Equality belongs to the upper branch.

steps.label: The step function turns a sum into zero or one · 2
steps.speakerNotes: Exactly zero also outputs one.

steps.label: Inputs one, zero, one add up to two · 1
steps.speakerNotes: The three inputs are one, zero, one, with all weights one. Their contributions are one, zero, one. Two active inputs each contribute one, so the sum is two. The dashed slot marks zero contribution.

steps.label: Inputs one, zero, one add up to two · 2
steps.speakerNotes: The inactive input contributes zero.

steps.label: Keep the sum fixed and move the threshold · 1
steps.speakerNotes: All three blue bars are identical because the sum stays two. Moving the threshold gives pre-activation values one, zero, and minus one. Exactly zero still meets the condition.

steps.label: Keep the sum fixed and move the threshold · 2
steps.speakerNotes: Thresholds one, two, three give outputs one, one, zero.

steps.label: AND needs both inputs to be one · 1
steps.speakerNotes: The axes are the two inputs. The four corners are all possible binary input pairs. Only the upper-right corner reaches a sum of two, so only that point is filled. The substitutions on the right verify each case.

steps.label: AND needs both inputs to be one · 2
steps.speakerNotes: AND: both conditions must hold.

steps.label: OR needs at least one input to be one · 1
steps.speakerNotes: Lower the threshold to one. The two corners with exactly one active input lie on the boundary and therefore output one. The all-zero corner remains below the threshold.

steps.label: OR needs at least one input to be one · 2
steps.speakerNotes: OR: at least one condition must hold.

steps.label: Lowering the threshold turns AND into OR · 1
steps.speakerNotes: Both diagrams use the same axes, four input points, and weights. Only the threshold changes, moving the line down and left. The two single-active-input corners now reach the threshold.

steps.label: Lowering the threshold turns AND into OR · 2
steps.speakerNotes: The inputs and weights stay fixed; the boundary moves.

steps.label: A negative weight reverses the response · 1
steps.speakerNotes: This added example from the lecture has one input. Set its weight to minus one and its bias to one half. Raising the input from zero to one lowers pre-activation from positive one half to negative one half, reversing the output.

steps.label: A negative weight reverses the response · 2
steps.speakerNotes: Added: a positive weight cannot implement NOT.

steps.label: Computing logic is not the same as learning · 1
steps.speakerNotes: McCulloch and Pitts proposed the early model in 1943. Here a person sets the weights in advance. Computing logic does not mean the model can adjust its own parameters. The perceptron will introduce learning from data.

steps.label: Computing logic is not the same as learning · 2
steps.speakerNotes: Next: use data to change the weights.

steps.label: Practice: add first, then test the threshold · 1
steps.speakerNotes: Use inputs one, one, zero, all weights one, and threshold two. Write the weighted sum, subtract the threshold, and apply the step function. Give students time to work it out.

steps.label: Practice: add first, then test the threshold · 2
steps.speakerNotes: Hint: find the sum, then subtract the threshold.

steps.label: Practice: choose a threshold for two active inputs · 1
steps.speakerNotes: The desired behavior is to fire when at least two inputs are active. Compare the two input patterns, choose a threshold that separates them, and check the remaining binary patterns.

steps.label: Practice: choose a threshold for two active inputs · 2
steps.speakerNotes: Hint: compare two active inputs with one active input.

steps.label: Practice: why can positive weights not make NOT? · 1
steps.speakerNotes: The left shows the desired NOT behavior. The direction on the right is intentionally left open. Ask how a positive weight changes the sum when the input rises, then compare with the required behavior.

steps.label: Practice: why can positive weights not make NOT? · 2
steps.speakerNotes: Hint: when the input rises, which way does the sum move?

steps.label: Self-check: which part integrates the signals? · 1
steps.speakerNotes: The options are dendrites, synapse, soma, and axon. Recall the role of each part and select the one that integrates incoming signals.

steps.label: Self-check: which part integrates the signals? · 2
steps.speakerNotes: Hint: where do the signals accumulate?

steps.label: Self-check: what does an artificial neuron copy? · 1
steps.speakerNotes: The alternatives are cell metabolism, accumulation and threshold firing, the neuron’s shape, and DNA copying. Explain the choice in terms of the computation.

steps.label: Self-check: what does an artificial neuron copy? · 2
steps.speakerNotes: Hint: look for the computation, not just the shape.

steps.label: Self-check: who proposed the model, and when? · 1
steps.speakerNotes: This question keeps the four name-and-year options from the source. Identify the origin of the McCulloch–Pitts model and distinguish it from later models and discussions.

steps.label: Self-check: who proposed the model, and when? · 2
steps.speakerNotes: Hint: recall the early model with fixed weights.

steps.label: Self-check: which activation function is used here? · 1
steps.speakerNotes: The four graphs show sigmoid, ReLU, binary step, and tanh. Compare their output values and behavior at zero, rather than choosing by name alone.

steps.label: Self-check: which activation function is used here? · 2
steps.speakerNotes: Hint: the output has only two possible values.
